final_recommendation: The room converged on a trilateral package framework with binding labor enforcement text, 5-year auto phase-in, and 16-year auto-renew sunset clause, scheduled for skeleton delivery at 8 AM and Friday signing. However, two critical gaps remain unresolved: (1) the dairy access floor (Canada at 3.25%, USTR demanding 3.75%), and (2) whether the labor enforcement tariff snapback triggers unilaterally or can be delayed by Mexican arbitration—both must be clarified in the skeleton text before the deal closes.
minority_objections: Canada objected that 3.75% dairy access erodes supply management beyond defensible limits
Dairy/Ag demanded confirmation that dairy opening is a binding condition, not a future negotiation
Auto/Labor/Supply-chain demanded clarity on whether tariff snapback is truly unilateral or can be disputed by Mexico
key_conflicts: Dairy access floor: Canada at 3.25% vs. USTR demanding 3.75% minimum
Labor enforcement trigger mechanism: whether tariff snapback is unilateral U.S. action or subject to Mexican arbitration
Timeline pressure: Mexico wants Friday signing, Canada needs skeleton verification at 8 AM before moving on dairy
key_concessions: Canada agreed to table limited dairy access (3.25%) after skeleton verification, breaking her initial 'supply management untouchable' position
USTR locked 'new assembly' labor-content definition to direct assembly labor only, carving out rework and sub-assembly
Mexico accepted 16-year auto-renew sunset language instead of hard termination
Auto industry accepted 5-year phase-in on 40% labor content with binding enforcement
red_lines: Canada: Chapter 19 dispute settlement stays intact (stated multiple times, never challenged)
USTR: 3.75% dairy access as stated floor (though Congress suggested 3.25% might be ratifiable)
Mexico: $16 wage floor and 40% labor content locked, no reopening
Labor/Congress: tariff snapback must be automatic without arbitration delays
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Enforcement trigger ambiguity: multiple agents demanded clarity on whether Mexico can delay tariff snapback via arbitration, but USTR never definitively answered whether it's truly unilateral
Dairy gap political risk: Congress suggested 3.25% vs 3.75% is 'not a deal-breaker,' but USTR maintained 3.75% as floor—no reconciliation occurred
Auto-renew sunset mechanism: USTR unilaterally locked this in without full Canadian input, raising ratification risk that was flagged but not resolved
downstream_risk_variables: Whether skeleton text at 8 AM specifies unilateral U.S. tariff trigger or allows Mexican dispute window
Whether USTR will actually ratify at 3.25% dairy or holds firm at 3.75%
Whether Congress accepts 16-year auto-renew language or demands renegotiation trigger at year 14
Whether Canadian government can defend 3.25% dairy concession domestically
uncertainty_notes: Two critical ambiguities remain for the 8 AM skeleton: (1) the enforcement snapback mechanism—whether it is truly unilateral U.S. action within 48 hours or subject to Mexican arbitration, and (2) the final dairy access number—whether USTR will ratify at Canada's 3.25% offer or holds firm at 3.75%. Both were demanded by multiple agents but never definitively answered by USTR. Additionally, the 16-year auto-renew sunset was locked unilaterally by USTR, raising ratification risk that Congress and Auto flagged but did not resolve.

marker_evidence.auto_rules_bottleneck: Auto RVC and labor-content stacking drove multiple rounds of negotiation—Canada demanded math verification, Auto/Labor demanded 'new assembly' definition be airtight, USTR locked 5-year phase-in as concrete proposal to close the deal
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_key: Labor enforcement mechanism (independent Mexican audits, automatic tariff snapback) was the primary stated condition for Congress ratification and drove USTR's binding-text commitment and Canada's willingness to move on dairy
marker_evidence.canada_dairy_final_issue: Dairy access became the final blocking item—Canada's 3.25% vs USTR's 3.75% floor remained unresolved at close, with Dairy/Ag stating 'my members won't ratify' without concrete opening and Canada saying 3.75% 'erodes supply management beyond defensible limits'
marker_evidence.dispute_settlement_canada_redline: Chapter 19 mentioned twice by Canada as 'stays intact, non-negotiable' but never challenged or discussed by others—acknowledged background constraint, not a negotiation driver
marker_evidence.sunset_to_review_compromise: Sunset clause discussed extensively (16-year auto-renew vs hard termination, year-14 renegotiation trigger) and shaped proposals, but did not drive the final outcome—USTR unilaterally locked 16-year auto-renew, raising ratification risk rather than resolving it
marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress ratification risk was a decisive constraint—drove USTR's binding labor text commitment, forced clarity on enforcement snapback timing, and shaped dairy negotiation (Congress stated 3.25% might be ratifiable, pressuring USTR's 3.75% floor)
marker_evidence.supply_chain_adjustment: Supply-chain concerns raised repeatedly (retooling timelines, capex planning, sourcing shifts) and drove 5-year phase-in proposal, but did not change the core deal terms—acknowledged and accommodated, not decisive
marker_evidence.us_mexico_first_pressures_canada: U.S.-Mexico bilateral forming first was explicit leverage—Mexico stated 'come in on these terms or we walk back to bilateral,' USTR threatened 'watch your auto plants negotiate directly with Mexico,' and this pressure drove Canada's conditional commitment to table dairy access
